proofs.proof_tex:
For the mixed family, let \(X\) be uniform, let \(\zeta\) be centered logistic and independent of \(X\), draw \(A\mid X=x\) with success probability \(x^{3/2}/2\), and put \(Y(a)=a+X+\zeta\).  Consistency holds by the definition of \(Y\), and independence of \(\zeta\) from the treatment draw gives unconfoundedness.  Positivity holds away from the two null endpoints.  For \(0<t<1/2\),
\[
 F_1^\pi(t)=P\{X\le(2t)^{2/3}\}=2^{2/3}t^{2/3}.
\]
Thus \(\gamma_1=5/3\), \(c_1=2^{2/3}\), and the Hall remainder is zero.  Since \(\pi_0\ge1/2\), \(\gamma_0=\infty\) and \(E_P(1/\pi_0)\le2\).

Take \(g_1=-\log2\) and \(g_0(x)=\log(1-x^{3/2}/2)\).  Then the former paired links hold, and \(\text{lem:paired-links-imply-joint-logit}\) gives
\[
 \eta(x)=\frac32\log x-\log(2-x^{3/2}),
 \qquad (\pi_1,\pi_0)=(\Lambda(\eta),\Lambda(-\eta)).
\]
Both \(g_a\) lie in a fixed \(C^{3/2}\) ball.  Opposite overlap holds near zero because \(\pi_1\le1/2\).

Writing \(\lambda(z)=e^{-z}(1+e^{-z})^{-2}\),
\[
 f_{a\mid X}(y\mid x)=\lambda(y-a-x),
 \qquad
 m_{a,\tau}(x)=\tau-\Lambda\{q_a(\tau)-a-x\}.
\]
Boundedness of \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda'\) gives the common conditional-density and score moduli.  Also
\[
 f_a(\tau)=\int_0^1\lambda\{q_a(\tau)-a-x\}\,dx>0,
\]
and finiteness of \(\mathcal A\times\mathcal T\) gives a positive common minimum.  Given \(\pi_1(X)=t\), \(X=(2t)^{2/3}\); hence the Lipschitz property of \(\Lambda\) gives
\[
 |\kappa_{1,\tau}(t)-\kappa_{1,\tau}(0)|
 \le \|\lambda\|_\infty(2t)^{2/3}.
\]
Taking \(G_1\) as the law of \(1+\zeta\) verifies the endpoint mark condition.  Symmetry of \(X+\zeta\) about \(1/2\) yields \(q_1(1/2)=3/2\), and
\[
 m^{\mathrm{tail}}_{1,1/2}=\frac12-\Lambda(1/2)\ne0.
\]

For the two-heavy family, retain the outcome construction and take the displayed odds.  Then
\[
 \eta(x)=\alpha_1\log x-\alpha_0\log(1-x),
\]
so the joint boundary link holds with \(g_0=g_1=0\).  At zero, \(\pi_1(x)=x^{\alpha_1}\{1+O(x^{\min(1,\alpha_1)})\}\); at one, \(\pi_0(x)=(1-x)^{\alpha_0}\{1+O((1-x)^{\min(1,\alpha_0)})\}\).  Monotone inversion under the uniform design gives
\[
 F_a^\pi(t)=c_at^{1/\alpha_a}\{1+O(t^{\rho_a})\},
 \qquad \gamma_a=1+\alpha_a^{-1}\in(1,2).
\]
Compactness supplies common constants and moduli.  The endpoints are disjoint, so opposite overlap holds on fixed endpoint neighborhoods.  The preceding logistic outcome calculations verify the remaining outcome and mark assumptions.  Thus both families belong to \(\mathcal P_{\mathrm S}\).

Write \(w(x)=\pi_0(x)\pi_1(x)\), \(\ell_1(x)=\log x\), and \(\ell_0(x)=\log(1-x)\).  The canonical chart, the joint boundary link, boundedness of \(g_1-g_0\), and positivity imply uniform constants \(0<c<C<\infty\) such that
\[
 c x^{\alpha_1}(1-x)^{\alpha_0}le w(x)le
 C x^{\alpha_1}(1-x)^{\alpha_0},\qquad 0<x<1.
\tag{B1}
\]
Indeed, writing \(R=e^{g_1-g_0}x^{\alpha_1}(1-x)^{-\alpha_0}\), one has \(w=R/(1+R)^2\); comparison with \(x^{\alpha_1}(1-x)^{\alpha_0}\) follows separately on \([0,1/2]\) and \([1/2,1]\).  This is where the canonical chart and the common Hölder radius are used.

For one observation the joint Bernoulli log likelihood is \(A\eta-\log(1+e^\eta)\).  Direct differentiation in directions \(v,z\) gives
\[
 \dot\ell_\eta(v)=(A-\pi_1)v,
 \qquad
 -E_P\ddot\ell_\eta(v,z)=E_P\{w(X)v(X)z(X)\}.
\tag{B2}
\]
Thus the score is centered and the information inner product is \(\langle v,z\rangle_w=\int_0^1wvz\), with no inverse propensity factor.

Let \(I_j=((j-1)/J,j/J]\).  From (B1),
\[
 \mu_j:=\int_{I_j}w(x)\,dx
 \asymp J^{-1}(j/J)^{\alpha_1}\{(J-j+1)/J\}^{\alpha_0}.
\tag{B3}
\]
On each cell, rescaling \(u=Jx-j+1\) and finite-dimensional norm equivalence for degree-\(r\) polynomials yield, for \(s_J=\sum_jv_jB_{j,J}\),
\[
 c\sum_j\mu_jv_j^2\le\|s_J\|_w^2\le C\sum_j\mu_jv_j^2.
\tag{B4}
\]
The constants are uniform because the spline degree is fixed and adjacent \(\mu_j\)'s have bounded ratios.

We now profile both logarithms.  Let \(\Pi_J\) be weighted projection on the spline space and \(r_{a,J}=(I-\Pi_J)\ell_a\).  On the first cell, \(\ell_1=-\log J+\log u\), the constant is in the spline space, and \(\log u\) has strictly positive distance from the polynomials of degree \(r\) in \(L^2(u^{\alpha_1}du)\).  Hence
\[
 \|r_{1,J}\|_w^2\ge cJ^{-(\alpha_1+1)}.
\tag{B5}
\]
Piecewise Taylor approximation on all later cells and the same first-cell rescaling give the reverse inequality.  Thus \(\|r_{1,J}\|_w^2\asymp J^{-(\alpha_1+1)}\).  Reflection gives
\[
 \|r_{0,J}\|_w^2\asymp J^{-(\alpha_0+1)}.
\tag{B6}
\]
For a linear combination, the nonsingular \(\log u\) residual occurs on the first cell only through the coefficient of \(\ell_1\), and on the last cell only through the coefficient of \(\ell_0\).  The other logarithm is analytic there; its degree-\(r\) Taylor remainder is \(O(J^{-(r+1)})\).  Since \(2r+1>\alpha_\star\), these cross remainders are of smaller squared order than (B5)--(B6).  Therefore
\[
 \|(I-\Pi_J)(c_1\ell_1-c_0\ell_0)\|_w^2
 \ge c\{c_1^2J^{-(\alpha_1+1)}+c_0^2J^{-(\alpha_0+1)}\}.
\tag{B7}
\]
Equations (B4) and (B7), by the Schur-complement identity for profiling, imply for the full coefficient vector \(u\)
\[
 u^TE_P\{w(X)Z_J(X)Z_J(X)^T\}u
 \ge cJ^{-(\alpha_\star+1)}\|u\|_2^2,
\tag{B8}
\]
where \(Z_J=(\ell_1,-\ell_0,B_{1,J},\ldots,B_{J,J})^T\).

The clipped logarithms differ from the true logarithms only on sets of length \(N^{-b_0}\).  Since \(b_0>1\), an iid training or evaluation sample hits either set with probability at most \(2N^{1-b_0}=o(1)\).  For the empirical Hessian, only \(O(J)\) pairs of spline coordinates overlap.  For each such pair, scalar Bernstein's exponential-moment argument applied to the bounded summands gives relative error
\[
 O_P\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{n\mu_j}}+\frac{\log n}{n\mu_j}\right).
\tag{B9}
\]
The same calculation for the two profiled log residuals costs at most two additional powers of \(\log n\).  Since \(\min_j\mu_j\asymp J^{-(\alpha_\star+1)}\), the stated global condition makes (B9) uniformly \(o_P(1)\).  Equations (B4)--(B7), applied after a union bound over the fixed-width spline bands and the four log blocks, show that the empirical Hessian lies between one half and twice its population counterpart with probability tending uniformly to one.

Choose the spline quasi-interpolant \(g_J\) of \(g_1-g_0\).  Hölder smoothness and \(r+1\ge s\) give \(\|g_J-(g_1-g_0)\|_\infty\le CJ^{-s}\).  On the boundary cells its Taylor remainder is \(O(J^{-s}u^s)\); dividing its inner product with the profiled log residual by (B5) or (B6) therefore gives an \(O(J^{-s})\) population profiling bias, not the cruder inverse-eigenvalue bound.  The compact parameter box contains this candidate for all large \(J\).

The score variance in any direction equals its information norm by (B2).  Solving the fixed-band empirical normal equations using (B3)--(B9), and then the two profiled equations using (B5)--(B7), yields on cell \(I_j\)
\[
 \sup_{x\in I_j}|\widehat\eta(x)-\eta(x)|
 =O_P\!\left((\log n)^C\left[J^{-s}+(n\mu_j)^{-1/2}\right]\right).
\tag{B10}
\]
This follows directly by multiplying the centered score on cell \(j\), whose variance is \(\mu_j/n\), by the inverse local information \(O(\mu_j^{-1})\); finite overlap in (B4) bounds the neighboring terms, while (B7) bounds the two profile coefficients.  The ridge derivative is \(O(e^{-J}J\sqrt J)\), smaller than every displayed order.  Concavity and empirical Hessian coercivity keep the maximizer in this local neighborhood, so the compact constraints are inactive asymptotically.

For arm \(a\), differentiation of \(\log\pi_a\) with respect to \(\eta\) multiplies by the opposite propensity and has absolute value at most one.  Near arm \(a\)'s zero endpoint this multiplier is bounded below; near the other endpoint it cancels the small information weight.  Applying (B10), (B3), and reflection gives
\[
 \sup_{d_a(x)\ge n^{-b_0}}|\log\widehat\pi_a(x)-\log\pi_a(x)|
 =O_P\!\left((\log n)^C\delta_{a,n}\right).
\tag{B11}
\]

For the signed functional, its derivative in a log-odds direction \(v\) is
\[
 \dot L_{1,\tau}(v)=\int m_{1,\tau}\pi_0v,
 \qquad
 \dot L_{0,\tau}(v)=-\int m_{0,\tau}\pi_1v.
\tag{B12}
\]
The information-space Riesz functions are consequently \(m_{1,\tau}/\pi_1\) and \(-m_{0,\tau}/\pi_0\).  Truncating them to the sieve and summing (B3) cellwise gives, for a heavy arm,
\[
 \|r_{a,\tau,J}\|_w^2\le CJ^{\alpha_a-1}.
\tag{B13}
\]
The score equation in this single direction, its variance identity, the \(J^{-s}\) profiling bias, and the quadratic Taylor remainder from (B10) give
\[
 L_{a,\tau}(\widehat\pi)-L_{a,\tau}(\pi)
 =O_P\!\left((\log n)^C\left[J^{-s}+n^{-1/2}J^{(\alpha_a-1)/2}+J^{\alpha_a}/n\right]\right).
\tag{B14}
\]
The last order follows from
\(\sum_{j=1}^J J^{\alpha_a}/(nj^{\alpha_a})=O(J^{\alpha_a}/n)\) when \(\alpha_a>1\).  The identical cell sum without the signed Riesz direction gives
\[
 \int\{(\widehat\pi_a-\pi_a)/\pi_a\}^2dP_X
 =O_P\!\left((\log n)^C[J^{-2s}+J^{\alpha_a}/n]\right).
\tag{B15}
\]

There is no evaluation point in either clipped coordinate set with probability tending to one, so (B11) implies \(E_{a,n}=O_P((\log n)^C\delta_{a,n})\).  Split \(D_{a,n}\) at \(u=M_n/h_{a,n}\).  Conditional on the training sample, its mean is bounded by \((n/h_{a,n})\) times (B14), plus \(CE_{a,n}M_n^{1/\alpha_a}\); the Hall identity \(c_an h_{a,n}^{-\gamma_a}\to1\) is used here.  Its conditional variance is bounded by
\[
 C(\log n)^C
 \left(J_n^{-2s}+\frac{J_n^{\alpha_a+1}}n\right)
 M_n^{-(\alpha_a-1)/\alpha_a}.
\tag{B16}
\]
To see (B16), use
\[
 \operatorname{Var}(D_{a,n}\mid\text{training})
 \le\frac n{h_{a,n}^2}\int_u^1
 \frac{\{\log\widehat\pi_a-\log\pi_a\}^2}{t}\,dF_a^\pi(t),
\]
insert (B10) on the first boundary cell, and integrate \(t^{-1}dF_a^\pi(t)\asymp t^{1/\alpha_a-2}dt\).  The lower endpoint contributes \((M_n/h_{a,n})^{1/\alpha_a-1}\).  Since \(h_{a,n}\asymp n^{\alpha_a/(\alpha_a+1)}\), multiplication by \(n/h_{a,n}^2\) cancels the remaining power of \(n\) and gives (B16).  The displayed tuning conditions make the conditional mean and variance vanish, proving the two transfer conclusions.

For \(J=n^\xi\), \(\delta_{a,n}=n^{-e_a(\xi)}\) up to logarithms.  Thus \(M_n=n^\lambda\) satisfies the amplification and tail-band conditions when \(0<\lambda<\min_a\{\alpha_ae_a(\xi),\alpha_a/(\alpha_a+1)\}\); (B16) then vanishes automatically.  The final interval for \(\xi\) handles (B14) and the global Hessian.  At \(\alpha_a=\alpha_\star=s=3/2\), \(\xi=3/10\) gives exponents \(-1/8\), \(-17/40\), and, after multiplication by \(n/h\), \(-1/40\), as claimed.

On the mixed center, \(\pi_0(x)=1-x^{3/2}/2\).  Direct inversion gives
\[
 F_0^\pi(t)=0\quad(t\le1/2),
 \qquad
 F_0^\pi(t)=1-\{2(1-t)\}^{2/3}\quad(1/2<t<1),
\]
so \(F_0^\pi(1/2+v)=4v/3+O(v^2)\).  The generalized-inverse equation yields \(t_{0,n}=1/2+3/(2n)+O(n^{-2})\) and \(h_{0,n}\to2\).

For the corrected joint likelihood, the mixed model has \(\alpha_1=3/2\), \(\alpha_0=0\), and \(\alpha_\star=3/2\).  The first and last cell calculations (B3)--(B10) in \(\text{lem:boundary-likelihood}\), now used with the displayed schedule, imply
\[
 \max_{1\le i\le n}|\widehat\eta_{-k(i)}(X_i)-\eta(X_i)|
 =O_P\!\left((\log n)^C\left[J_n^{-s}+\sqrt{J_n^{5/2}/n}\right]\right)=o_P(1).
\]
The endpoint clipping of the log regressors is irrelevant with probability tending to one because \(P\{\min_i(X_i\wedge(1-X_i))<n^{-b_0}\}\le2n^{1-b_0}\).  Since \(\Lambda\) is \(1/4\)-Lipschitz,
\[
 \max_i|\widehat\pi_{0,-k(i)}(X_i)-\pi_0(X_i)|=o_P(1).
\]
The fitted empirical distribution is therefore sandwiched between vanishing translates of the empirical distribution of \(\pi_0(X)\).  The law of large numbers at continuity points and the preceding population inversion give \(\widehat h_{0,n}\to_P2\).  Every fixed lower order statistic of \(\pi_0(X_i)\) tends to \(1/2\); the tight random rank \(\lceil\widehat h_{0,n}\rceil\) and uniform fitted error consequently give
\[
 \widehat p_{0,(\lceil\widehat h_{0,n}\rceil)}\to_P1/2,
 \qquad \widehat b_{0,n}\to_P\vartheta_0/2<1/2.
\]
Because \(k_n/n\to0\), the largest \(k_n+1\) values of \(Z_{0,i}=1/\widehat\pi_0(X_i)\) converge uniformly to two.  Their Hill log-spacing average tends to zero, so its reciprocal diverges and \(\widehat\gamma_0\to_P\infty\).  The control arm is therefore classified Gaussian and its correction is zero with probability tending to one.  Finally, the fitted minimum converges to \(1/2\) while the clip converges to a strict smaller value, so all clipped weights equal the untrimmed fitted weights with probability tending to one.

Uniform Hall inversion gives
\[
 c_{a,P}nt_{a,P,n}^{\gamma_{a,P}}=1+o(1),
 \qquad h_{a,P,n}=(c_{a,P}n)^{1/\gamma_{a,P}}\{1+o(1)\}.
\tag{H1}
\]
For \(Z_i=h_{a,P,n}\pi_a(X_i)\) and \(U_i=\Psi_a(Y_i)\), consistency, unconfoundedness, Hall regular variation, and \(\text{lem:score-law-factorization}\) imply, for compactly supported continuous \(g\),
\[
 nE_P[\mathbf1\{A_i=a\}g(Z_i,U_i)]
 \to\int_0^\infty\int g(z,u)H_{a,P}(du)(\gamma_{a,P}-1)z^{\gamma_{a,P}-1}dz.
\tag{H2}
\]
The iid Laplace identity turns (H2) into uniform convergence of the marked point process.  Truncation at \(z<c\) and \(z>C\) is uniform because the corresponding bounds are \(Cc^{1+\epsilon_\gamma}\) and \(CC^{-\epsilon_\gamma}\).  Hence the centered population-clipped score in \(\text{def:oracle-leading-statistic}\) converges uniformly in bounded-Lipschitz distance to \(\mathsf Z_{a,\theta,P}/f_{a,P}=L_{a,P}\).

The uncentered clipped score has mean
\[
 \frac n{h_{a,n}}E_Pm_{a,\tau}(X)
 \left\{\frac{\pi_a(X)}{\pi_a(X)\vee\theta_a/h_{a,n}}-1\right\}
 \to-\frac{\theta_a^{\gamma_a-1}}{\gamma_a}m^{\mathrm{tail}}_{a,\tau}
 =\mu_{a,\theta}(\tau),
\tag{H3}
\]
where direct integration of \((z/\theta_a-1)(\gamma_a-1)z^{\gamma_a-2}\) on \((0,\theta_a)\) gives the sign and constant.  The count sandwich from \(E_{a,n}M_n^{\gamma_a-1}=o_P(1)\) gives \(\widehat h_{a,n}/h_{a,n}\to_P1\) and \(\widehat h_{a,n}\widehat b_{a,n}\to_P\vartheta_a\).  Splitting the feasible score at \(M_n/h_{a,n}\), the tail difference is \(O_P(E_{a,n}M_n^{\gamma_a-1})\), and the interior difference is \(D_{a,n}=o_P(1)\).  Thus the feasible score is samplewise \(o_P(1)\) from its population-clipped counterpart.

Knight's identity (G5), the conditional-density modulus, and \(h_{a,n}/n\to0\) give deterministic and centered remainders \(f_{a,P}(\tau)t^2/2+o_P(1)\), uniformly on compact \(t\)-sets.  The Hill, endpoint-score, and density estimators are consistent by the same count sandwich, the intermediate-order condition, the mark modulus, and the bandwidth conditions.  Therefore the empirical correction consistently subtracts (H3).  The common positive curvature and convex argmin comparison yield
\[
 \max_{\tau\in\mathcal T}\left|
 \frac n{h_{a,P,n}}\{\widehat q_a^{\mathrm{bc}}(\tau)-q_{a,P}(\tau)\}
 -\mathsf S_{a,P,n}(\tau)\right|=o_P(1)
\tag{H4}
\]
uniformly.  Equations (H2)--(H4) prove the stated uniform bounded-Lipschitz approximation and the fixed-law limit.  Removing the fitted-score comparison proves the true-propensity oracle version.  The endpoint input is only \(H_a\) by the established score-law factorization lemma.

Fix the heavy treated arm of the mixed nonzero-drift witness and write \(\epsilon_n=M_n^{-(\gamma_a-1)}\).  On the fitted tail band the corrected escape construction is not cut by its safety threshold with probability tending to one, because \(M_n/\widehat h_{a,n}\to_P0\).  Since \(E_{a,n}=o_P(\epsilon_n)\),
\[
 \frac{\widehat\pi^{\mathrm{esc}}_{a,-k}}{\pi_a}-1
 =\epsilon_n+o_P(\epsilon_n)
\]
on every strict sub-band.  Its sample count diverges by Hall regular variation, so \(E^{\mathrm{esc}}_{a,n}M_n^{\gamma_a-1}\to_P1\).  Above the band, only an asymptotically negligible shell differs, and the interior estimate in \(\text{lem:boundary-likelihood}\) gives \(D^{\mathrm{esc}}_{a,n}\to_P0\).  Since \(\epsilon_n\to0\), every fixed endpoint window keeps the same mark law.

For fixed \(C>\theta_a\), the conditional mean difference of normalized scores on \(C/h<\pi_a<M_n/h\) is
\[
 -\epsilon_n\frac n h\{1+o_P(1)\}
 \int_{C/h}^{M_n/h}\kappa_{a,\tau}(t)\,dF_a^\pi(t).
\]
Hall regular variation and the mark modulus make this converge to \(-m^{\mathrm{tail}}_{a,\tau}\), because \(c_an h^{-\gamma_a}\to1\) and \(\epsilon_nM_n^{\gamma_a-1}=1\).  Its conditional variance is \(o_P(1)\) by the same truncated calculation as (B16).  The drift estimators are unchanged to first order, and common multiplicative factors cancel from Hill spacings.  Positive-curvature argmin expansion therefore gives
\[
 \frac n{h_{a,n}}\{\widehat q_a^{\mathrm{bc,esc}}(\tau)-\widehat q_a^{\mathrm{bc}}(\tau)\}
 \to_P-\frac{m^{\mathrm{tail}}_{a,\tau}}{f_a(\tau)}.
\]
The target endpoint score is nonzero on the witness.  Thus the amplification order remains intrinsic under the binary-coherent perturbation.

Let \(s_v(O)=(A-\pi_1(X))v(X)\).  By (B2), its information is \(E_P\{\pi_0\pi_1v^2\}\).  For arm one the derivative of the propensity-induced signed functional is \(\int m_{1,\tau}\pi_0v\), so its Riesz function is \(r_{1,\tau}=m_{1,\tau}/\pi_1\).  For arm zero the derivative is \(-\int m_{0,\tau}\pi_1v\), so \(r_{0,\tau}=-m_{0,\tau}/\pi_0\).  In either case
\[
 E_Ps_{r_{a,\tau}}^2
 \le E_P\{1/\pi_a(X)\}\le C_{\mathrm G},
\tag{G1}
\]
using \(|m_{a,\tau}|\le1\) and \(\text{ass:finite-variance}\).  Thus the full Riesz functions exist for every Gaussian arm.

The score equations, averaged over cross-fitting folds, give
\[
 \sqrt n\sum_k\frac{|I_k|}{n}\dot L_{a,\tau}(\widehat\eta_{-k}-\eta)
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^ns_{r_{a,\tau}}(O_i)+o_P(1).
\tag{G2}
\]
The coefficient is one because an observation enters \(K-1\) training samples, each of size \(n(K-1)/K+O(1)\).  The remainder in (G2) is bounded by \(\sqrt nJ^{-2s}+J\log J/\sqrt n\), while empirical-Hessian replacement is controlled by \(J^{\alpha_\star+1}(\log n)^3/n\); all vanish by the stated schedule and (B3)--(B10).

We now compute the evaluation fluctuation without dropping its weights.  Conditionally on a training fold,
\[
 E_P\!\left[\pi_a(X)\{\widehat\pi_a(X)^{-1}-\pi_a(X)^{-1}\}^2\right]
 =E_P\!\left[\frac{\{\widehat\pi_a(X)-\pi_a(X)\}^2}
 {\pi_a(X)\widehat\pi_a(X)^2}\right].
\tag{G3}
\]
On the event (B11), the integrand is bounded by a constant times \((\widehat\eta-\eta)^2/\pi_a\) near arm \(a\)'s endpoint; the opposite endpoint is damped by the derivative of \(\log\pi_a\).  On cell \(j\) adjacent to the target endpoint, (B3) and (B10) give stochastic contribution
\[
 \frac{J^{2\alpha_a}}{n j^{2\alpha_a}}.
\tag{G4}
\]
Summing (G4) gives \(J/n\) when \(2\alpha_a<1\), \(J\log J/n\) when \(2\alpha_a=1\), and \(J^{2\alpha_a}/n\) when \(2\alpha_a>1\).  The Hölder approximation contributes \(J^{-2s}\int_0^1x^{-\alpha_a}dx=O(J^{-2s})\), because a finite-variance finite-index arm has \(\alpha_a<1\); the bounded branch has \(\alpha_a=0\).  This proves the displayed variance rate.  The global Hessian condition implies \(\mathfrak r_a(J_n)/n\to0\), because \(2\alpha_a<\alpha_\star+1\).

Knight's identity, verified by the three sign cases, is
\[
 \rho_\tau(e-v)-\rho_\tau(e)
 =-v\{\tau-\mathbf1(e\le0)\}
 +\int_0^v\{\mathbf1(e\le z)-\mathbf1(e\le0)\}\,dz.
\tag{G5}
\]
Apply it with \(v=t/\sqrt n\).  The conditional-density modulus gives curvature \(f_{a,P}(\tau)t^2/2+o_P(1)\), uniformly on compact \(t\)-sets.  Equations (G2)--(G4) make the centered cross-fit evaluation remainder \(o_P(1)\).  The linear term is
\[
 \frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n
 \left[\frac{\mathbf1\{A_i=a\}\psi_{a,\tau}(Y_i)}{\pi_a(X_i)}
 -s_{r_{a,\tau}}(O_i)\right].
\tag{G6}
\]
For \(a=1\), substituting \(r_{1,\tau}=m_{1,\tau}/\pi_1\) turns the bracket into
\[
 m_{1,  au}(X_i)+\frac{A_i\{\psi_{1,  au}(Y_i)-m_{1,  au}(X_i)\}}{\pi_1(X_i)}.
\]
For \(a=0\), substituting \(r_{0,  au}=-m_{0,  au}/\pi_0\) gives
\[
 m_{0,  au}(X_i)+\frac{(1-A_i)\{\psi_{0,  au}(Y_i)-m_{0,  au}(X_i)\}}{\pi_0(X_i)}.
\]
After division by \(f_a(\tau)\), these are exactly the declared influence functions.  Joint calculation retains \(E_P[\mathrm{IF}_{0,P}\mathrm{IF}_{1,P}^T]\); no separate-fit independence is asserted.

For finite \(\gamma_a\ge2+\epsilon_\gamma\), Hall integration yields
\[
 E_P\!\left[\pi_a(X)^{-1}\mathbf1\{\pi_a(X)^{-1}>z\}\right]
 \le Cz^{-(\gamma_a-2)}\le Cz^{-\epsilon_\gamma}.
\tag{G7}
\]
For \(\gamma_a=\infty\), the joint link and fixed Hölder radius give a common positive lower propensity bound.  Equation (G7) proves uniform Lindeberg for the finite influence vector.  Expanding scalar-projection characteristic functions to second order on the Lindeberg event gives uniform Gaussian bounded-Lipschitz approximation with the row covariance.

Hall integration also shows that population clipping has bias \(o(n^{-1/2})\) and centered variance \(o(1)\) uniformly when \(\gamma_a>2\); fitted-threshold consistency transfers this to the empirical clip.  The bounded branch follows from sample-point consistency.  Convexity, the common positive density lower bound, and (G5)--(G7) now give
\[
 \sqrt n(\widehat q_a-q_{a,P})
 =\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{IF}_{a,P}(O_i)+o_P(1)
\]
uniformly.  This leading sum is precisely \(\mathsf S_{a,P,n}\), proving the required samplewise approximation to \(\text{def:oracle-leading-statistic}\), its uniform law approximation to \(L_{a,P}\), and the fixed-law corollary.

Define \(W_{a,P,n}=nH_{a,P,n}^{-1}(\widehat q_a^{\mathrm{bc}}-q_{a,P})\).  Equations (H4) and the Gaussian samplewise expansion give
\[
 \max_a\|W_{a,P,n}-\mathsf S_{a,P,n}\|=o_P(1)
\tag{Q1}
\]
uniformly, while their point-process and Lindeberg calculations give uniform bounded-Lipschitz convergence of \(\mathsf S_{P,n}\) to \(L_P\).  Two heavy endpoint processes are independent in the limit because their canonical endpoint neighborhoods are disjoint.  A heavy and Gaussian coordinate are asymptotically independent after deleting the Gaussian summands on the shrinking heavy endpoint set; the deleted variance vanishes by Hall integration.  Two Gaussian coordinates retain \(E_P[\mathrm{IF}_{0,P}\mathrm{IF}_{1,P}^T]\).

The exact identity
\[
 \frac n{H_{P,n}}(\widehat\Delta^{\mathrm{bc}}-\Delta_P)
 =\ell_{1,P,n}W_{1,P,n}-\ell_{0,P,n}W_{0,P,n}
\]
and the analogous definition of \(Z_{P,n}\) transfer (Q1) through a map of Lipschitz norm at most two.  This proves uniform bounded-Lipschitz approximation without convergence of the weights.  For fixed \(P\), Hall inversion gives \(h_{a,P,n}\asymp n^{1/\gamma_{a,P}}\): the smaller unequal heavy index dominates, equal heavy indices retain both Hall constants, and a heavy scale dominates \(\sqrt n\).  Along convergent-weight subsequences, the continuous mapping theorem gives the stated fixed-law limit.

By \(\text{lem:oracle-leading-permutation-symmetry}\), \(\mathsf S_{P,m}\) is a symmetric measurable kernel of an \(m\)-sample.  For a bounded one-Lipschitz \(g\), let \(U_{n,m,P}(g)\) be the complete average of \(g(\mathsf S_{P,b})\) over all \(m\)-subsets.  The orthogonal Hoeffding decomposition, obtained by successive conditional centering, gives
\[
 \operatorname{Var}_P\{U_{n,m,P}(g)\}
 =\sum_{j=1}^m\frac{\binom mj^2}{\binom nj}\zeta_{P,m,j}
 \le\frac mn\operatorname{Var}_P\{g(\mathsf S_{P,m})\}
 \le4m/n.
\tag{S1}
\]
The inequality uses \(\binom mj/\binom nj\le m/n\).  Uniform tightness of the heavy point-process and Gaussian leading laws permits a finite bounded-Lipschitz net on a common compact set, so (S1) upgrades pointwise convergence to
\[
 d_{\mathrm{BL}}\{\mathcal L_B(\mathsf S_{P,B}\mid O_1^n),\mathcal L_P(L_P)\}=o_P(1)
\tag{S2}
\]
uniformly.  The unconditional law of a uniform \(m\)-subset is the iid \(m\)-sample law.  Hence the samplewise arm approximations at \(N=m\), Markov's inequality, and (S2) replace \(\mathsf S_{P,B}\) by the completely refitted arm vector.

Centering at the full estimator contributes
\[
 O_P\!\left(\frac m{H_{a,P,m}}\frac{H_{a,P,n}}n\right)
 =O_P\{(m/n)^{1-1/\gamma_a}\}
\]
on a heavy arm and \(O_P\{(m/n)^{1/2}\}\) on a Gaussian arm; gamma separation makes both uniform \(o_P(1)\).  Scale consistency gives \(\widehat\ell_{a,n}-\ell_{a,P,n}=o_P(1)\).  Recombination therefore proves the conditional bounded-Lipschitz approximation to \(Z_{P,n}\).

Half-line indicators are approximated above and below by Lipschitz ramps of width \(\eta\).  Apply this smoothing to the conditional approximation and the full-sample joint-QTE approximation, then let \(n\to\infty\) and \(\eta\downarrow0\).  The coordinate anti-concentration modulus gives the asymmetric pointwise coverage.  The map \(x\mapsto\|x\|_\infty\) is one-Lipschitz, so the maximum anti-concentration modulus gives simultaneous coverage for the finite set \(\mathcal T\).

For the internal diagnostic, choose a two-heavy row with \(\gamma_{0,P_n}=\gamma+c/(2\log n)\) and \(\gamma_{1,P_n}=\gamma-c/(2\log n)\).  Hall inversion gives
\[
 \log\{h_{0,P_n,n}/h_{1,P_n,n}\}\to-c/\gamma^2,
 \qquad
 \log\{h_{0,P_n,m}/h_{1,P_n,m}\}\to-\beta c/\gamma^2
\]
when \(m=n^\beta\).  Thus \(T^{\mathrm{raw}}_{B,n}\) uses a different arm mixture, whereas armwise standardization followed by full-sample recombination reproduces the first ratio.  This proves exactly the internal diagnostic stated, without attributing it to any published estimator.

added_lemmas.statement:
Suppose that \(\pi_0(x)+\pi_1(x)=1\), both propensities are positive, and, with \(\alpha_a=0\) on a bounded-support arm,
\[
 \pi_a(x)=d_a(x)^{\alpha_a}e^{g_a(x)},\qquad a\in\{0,1\},
\]
whenever \(d_0(x)d_1(x)>0\).  Then
\[
 \log\frac{\pi_1(x)}{\pi_0(x)}
 =\alpha_1\log d_1(x)-\alpha_0\log d_0(x)+g_1(x)-g_0(x),
\]
and \(\pi_1(x)=\Lambda\{\eta(x)\}\), \(\pi_0(x)=\Lambda\{-\eta(x)\}\).  Hence the joint log-odds representation contains every law satisfying the former paired links.
added_lemmas.proof_tex:
By positivity, both logarithms are finite off the two endpoints.  Taking logarithms of the paired links and subtracting gives
\[
 \log\pi_1(x)-\log\pi_0(x)
 =\alpha_1\log d_1(x)-\alpha_0\log d_0(x)+g_1(x)-g_0(x).
\]
The left side is \(\eta(x)\).  Since \(\pi_0=1-\pi_1\), exponentiation gives \(\pi_1/(1-\pi_1)=e^\eta\), and therefore
\[
 \pi_1=\frac{e^\eta}{1+e^\eta}=\Lambda(\eta),
 \qquad
 \pi_0=\frac1{1+e^\eta}=\Lambda(-\eta).
\]
Under the canonical uniform chart, the endpoints have \(P_X\)-measure zero, so arbitrary coherent endpoint values do not change the law.  This proves the claimed inclusion without adding a law restriction beyond the separately disclosed canonical-chart restriction.

proposed.name: Endpoint-safe joint cross-fitted logistic-series learner
proposed.construction:
For a generic fitting sample size \(N\in\{n,m\}\), put
\[
 L_{1,N}(x)=\log\{x\vee N^{-b_0}\},
 \qquad
 L_{0,N}(x)=\log\{(1-x)\vee N^{-b_0}\},
\]
and
\[
 \eta_{J_N}(x;\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\beta)
 =\alpha_1L_{1,N}(x)-\alpha_0L_{0,N}(x)
   +\sum_{j=1}^{J_N}\beta_jB_{j,J_N}(x),
 \qquad
 p_{J_N}(x;\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\beta)
 =\Lambda\{\eta_{J_N}(x;\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\beta)\}.
\]
Let \(\Theta_{J_N}=[0,J_N]^2\times[-J_N,J_N]^{J_N}\).  On a training sample excluding fold \(I_k\), define \((\widehat\alpha_{0,-k},\widehat\alpha_{1,-k},\widehat\beta_{-k})\) as the unique maximizer over \(\Theta_{J_N}\) of
\[
 \sum_{i\notin I_k}
 \left[A_i\log p_{J_N}(X_i;\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\beta)
 +(1-A_i)\log\{1-p_{J_N}(X_i;\alpha_0,\alpha_1,\beta)\}\right]
 -e^{-J_N}\left(\alpha_0^2+\alpha_1^2+sum_{j=1}^{J_N}\beta_j^2\right).
\]
The strictly concave ridge makes the maximizer unique; no global probability-range constraint is imposed.  Set
\[
 \widehat\eta_{-k}(x)=
 \eta_{J_N}(x;\widehat\alpha_{0,-k},\widehat\alpha_{1,-k},\widehat\beta_{-k}),
 \qquad
 \widehat\pi_{1,-k}(x)=\Lambda\{\widehat\eta_{-k}(x)\},
 \qquad
 \widehat\pi_{0,-k}(x)=1-\widehat\pi_{1,-k}(x).
\]
Thus the fitted probabilities are endpoint-safe and binary coherent.  At the full sample use \(N=n\), and in a refit use its actual size \(N=m\).
